metadata.description: Hamdane Ben Othman Khodja (1773- entre 1840 et 1845) était un notable et un savant d'Alger . Il a écrit Le Miroir dans lequel il dénonce les exactions des soldats français à Alger peu après la conquête de l'Algérie par la France. Hamdane Ben Othman Khodja appartient à une famille de notables algérois, son père, Othman, un jurisconsulte de renom, jouissait d’une grande estime auprès de l’administration de la Régence d'Alger, représentée à sa plus haute échelle par le dey. Ayant montré des compétences inouïes en matière de lois, le dey lui confia la supervision des comptes budgétaires et les dossiers contenant les noms et les grades, ainsi que les traitements des janissaires. En plus de l’administration, le père de Hamdane exerçait également le métier d’enseignant qu’il transmettra plus tard à son fils. Son oncle Mohammed Hadj, quant à lui, s’occupait de Dar El Seka, l’équivalent de l’Hôtel des Monnaies de nos jours.   Khodja est né à Alger en 1773 dans une famille d'origine turque appartenant à la haute administration de la régence d'Alger . Son père était un lettré koloughli, un ouléma et le defterdar de la Régence, et sa mère, une mauresque. Il reçut une excellente éducation et voyagea beaucoup . En 1784, lorsque son oncle eut la responsabilité de porter un cadeau du dey à Istanbul, il l'accompagna. Après son retour d’Istanbul, Hamdane passa à une étape supérieure de son apprentissage, il se consacra ainsi à l’étude de la philosophie, de la théologie et des sciences de son temps. La médecine occupait une partie importante de cette passion dévouée au savoir. Il écrira plus tard un ouvrage traitant des moyens de se prémunir de l’épidémie et qu’il intitula Ithaf al mounsifin wa el odaba fi el ihtiraz min el ouaba (Le don fait aux justes et aux lettrés pour se prémunir des maladies épidémiques). Après la mort de son père, il lui succéda comme enseignant en théologie puis rapidement son oncle le prit dans son affaire et l'envoya le représenter dans des villes comme Tunis, Livourne, Marseille, Londres et Gibraltar, lui donnant ainsi l'occasion d'apprendre le turc, le français et l'anglais . Khodja devint un des marchands les plus importants et les plus riches d'Alger, où il était très sollicité par des collègues désireux d'être associés à ses opérations commerciales qui s'étendaient à l'empire ottoman comme à l'Europe .     Après l’occupation d’Alger, il fut nommé membre de la municipalité que Bourmont constitua. Selon H. Khodja, ce n’était qu’une mascarade, car : « Les délibérations étaient silencieuses et pour la forme ; enfin notre participation était nulle au fond ». En sa qualité de membre du conseil municipal d'Alger ,il participa à la commission française d'indemnisation des personnes dont les biens avaient été démolis pour cause "d'utilité publique" jusqu'à la dissolution de cette commission et la fin des indemnisations. Il servit ensuite d'intermédiaire entre le bey de Constantine, Hadj Ahmed et les Français   Face aux exactions commises par les troupes françaises, il rédigea en 1833 un manuscrit qui se voulait à la fois historique et politique, Aperçu historique et statistique sur la régence d’Alger, intitulé en arabe al Mir’āt’ (Le Miroir). Un témoignage qui demeure avant tout, un plaidoyer et un réquisitoire : un plaidoyer en faveur de la Régence et un réquisitoire contre l’administration de Bourmont et de Clauzel. Le manuscrit a été écrit par lui en arabe, et a été traduit en français par H.-D. Oriental et publié à Paris en 1833 aux éditons Goetchy fils et Cie; sous le titre [Aperçu historique et statistique sur la régence d'Alger, intitulé en arabe : "Le Miroir" ; par sidy Hamdan-Ben-Othman-Khoja,... Traduit de l'arabe par H.... D..  1833.  ]   Une "Réfutation de l'ouvrage de Sidi Hamdan" parut dans l'Observateur des Tribunaux en 1834 à quoi Hamdan Khodja répliqua, la même année et dans la même revue, par une "Réponse au maréchal Clauzel", ce dernier étant vraisemblablement l'auteur de la "réfutation" Les initiales H.-D. poussent à croire que le travail de traduction fut l’œuvre du Tripolitain (Tripoli d’al Gharb)  : Hassouna Daghiss (Hassuna D’ghies.). Pourtant, Personne ne peut affirmer ni infirmer, si c’est bien lui l’auteur de la traduction, car H. Khodja, lui-même, ne le confirme pas. Ce dernier, dans une lettre datée du 28 décembre 1833 qu’il adresse au général Voirol, écrivit que l’ouvrage a été imprimé à Paris et, que son fils Hassan en aurait reçu un exemplaire qu’il devait remettre à la Commission [ Commission d’Afrique, créée pour enquêter sur la situation en Algérie ] . Chose qui n’a pas pu se faire car le livre arriva tardivement. Par contre, il ordonna à son fils de le remettre au général afin qu’il examine son travail : « J’ai donné ordre à mon fils de vous le remettre et je réclame .de votre justice d’examiner ce travail sans faire attention à son auteur, car chacun écrit d’après l’éducation qu’il a reçu et de son propre jugement ». D’ailleurs, ce qui est singulier c’est que dans le Miroir, il ne fait aucune allusion à l’aide que lui aurait apportée Daghiss : en effet, la seule fois où il parle de lui, c’est quand il souligne la traduction que fit ce dernier de l’œuvre de Vattel, traduction qu’il a fait du français vers l’arabe. le mémoire a été publié en annexe du livre de Michel Habart intitulé  "Histoire d'un parjure". La question est : pourquoi ne l’a-t-il pas clairement spécifié, étant donné qu’il ne manque pas de le féliciter pour son travail de traducteur : « Je ne lis pas le français, cependant j’ai bien connaissance de la traduction fidèle en arabe, que M. le chérif Hassuna Deguiz a faite du droit des gens de Wattel ». Le texte original en arabe du Miroir n’a jamais été retrouvé, seule la version en français existe ; et c’est à partir de cette dernière, qu’il fut traduit, présenté et commenté en langue arabe par Mohamed Larbi Z’biri. [ ( 1985), Al Mir‛āt  Alger, SNED. ] Sans mettre en doute l’authenticité ou réfuter l’ouvrage ,l’original aurait mieux permis d’appréhender toute la richesse du texte et d’en exploiter les idées et, surtout de mettre fin aux doutes et aux rumeurs qui supposaient que le manuscrit avait été écrit par un publiciste français, donc n’aurait jamais été traduit. D’autre part, il existe une autre publication du Miroir où le texte est suivi d’une réfutation des amis du maréchal Clauzel ainsi que d’une réponse à la réfutation En 2009, lors du symposium organisé à Alger, portant sur thème « L’Algérie, durant la période ottomane : Les relations politiques, économiques et culturelles », les Archives Nationales d’Alger (A.N.A) se sont vues offrir par le gouvernement turc, deux manuscrits écrits en langue arabe. Le premier, intitulé  "Le Miroir d'Alger" (" مرآة الجزائر "), écrit en 1837 par Mohamed Redha, le fils de H. Khodja et le second est une copie d’un deuxième livre de H. Khodja dans lequel il traite et appuie les réformes engagées par le sultan ottoman, Abdelhamid II » Le Miroir se divise en deux parties. La première est répartie en douze chapitres, les six premiers sont consacrés à décrire le pays, les habitants en faisant d’eux des êtres attachants, respectueux de leurs traditions ancestrales. Nous remarquons que pour désigner les habitants : Algérois, Kabyles, Arabes, Turcs ou Kouloughlis, il utilise le mot « Algériens », est-ce à dire que déjà les notions d’État et de nation avaient pris forme dans son esprit, et que de ce fait, il pouvait les appliquer à la Régence en rassemblant les différentes communautés qui se côtoyaient sans vraiment avoir à l’esprit ce sentiment d’unité ? Était-il le seul à le penser ou bien d’autres partageaient-ils sa vision ? Car par rapport aux correspondances qu’il adressait à l’administration turque, et telles qu’elles ont été traduites en arabe, nous pouvons observer que les vocables utilisées généralement pour désigner les populations sont « ‛ahl » ou « raʽiyya » ou sujets ou tout simplement il oppose les musulmans aux infidèles. Les chapitres restants sont consacrés au gouvernement, à ses lois et à sa législation. Il insiste sur le fait que la Régence était un État fondé sur des principes républicains, qui n’a rien à voir avec un État corsaire sans foi ni loi comme le pensait l’Europe, Il écrit :   « Dans le cours de mon voyage en Europe, j’ai étudié les principes de la liberté européenne qui fait la base d’un gouvernement représentatif et républicain. J’ai trouvé que ces principes étaient semblables aux principes fondamentaux de notre législation, si ce n’est qu’il existe une différence imperceptible dans l’application ». Toutefois, il ne nie pas l’aspect négatif de certains deys, de leurs erreurs qui ont entrainé le déclin de l’État algérien et l’occupation française. La seconde partie relate le début de l’occupation française, de son administration et des erreurs tactiques et des exactions commises envers la population et ses biens. Il met l’accent sur les promesses non tenues de certains généraux, il les accuse d’avoir déshonoré leur intégrité ; c’est la partie miroir ou la partie négative de l’occupation, son but étant de faire passer un message libéral et de toucher l’opinion publique sur la question de l’indépendance de l’Algérie. Ce n’est plus le Turc ni le Kouloughli qui parle mais l’Algérien qui est attaché à sa patrie : » […] chez nous nous n’étions pas hommes d’ Etat , ce n’est que sur cette terre que nous avons acquis nos titres, et nos dignités… ; ce pays est donc notre patrie !  ». Avant de poursuivre, cette citation mérite que l’on s’y arrête, car elle soulève plusieurs interrogations par rapport à la perception de « patrie » qui elle-même renvoie à des interrogations sur les notions de peuple, de communauté et de nation. Ainsi, lorsque H. Khodja   parle de patrie il désignait sa terre natale, et par peuple(s) l’ensemble des communautés de la Régence qui formaient une nation, un peuple de tribus tous unis par leur attachement à leur terre. Après avoir en vain demandé au Sultan ottoman d'intervenir, il quitta Paris en 1836 pour s'établir à Istanbul où il mourut entre 1840 et 1845.

The three-year-old regime is looking increasingly shaky and after a series of purg~s of government officials, the 34-year-old president appears to have been the target of disaffected factions inside the country. "A coup could happen at any time," says a Yemeni close to the presidential palace. "Salih is now so isolated that every hand is turned against him." North Yemen has had a vialent past, but Salih, a former army lieutenant-colonel, has survived by a combination of political astuteness and a ruthless approach to any opposition. He has shrewdly played up the strategic importance of North Yemen to draw support from east and West while carefully maintaining some semblance of neutrality. Saudi Arabia, in particular is a close supporter and has been financing the bankrupt Yemeni economy. In return, the Saudis have expected Salih to remain pro-~Jest and distanced from Moscow and the Russian-backed regime in South Yemen. However, the Saudis have been unhappy about rumors of Salih's impending visit to rioscow which the president has been using to obtain increased aid from both the Saudis and the West. Also, Salih recently arrested the former foreign minister, 'Abdallah al-Asnaj, iaho is a close Saudi supporter. Salih threatened to execute Asnaj unless the Saudis increased their aid. The Saudis agreed, but Riyadh appears to have decided that Saleh has gone too far. "Salih is only hangir~g on because he has the support of the security police," said one North Yemeni. "The army, as usual, is waiting to see what will happen and dissidents are becoming incr.easingly active around San'a'." - The atmosphere in the capital is tense. description: CONTENTS. CHAPTER I. Germany, Trieste, and the Adriatic. Cologne, 2 ; Dresden, its Churches and Gallery, 3 ; The Church in Austria, 5 ; Neisse, 8 ; Pius Verein , or Church Union, 9 ; Reverential Demeanour at home and abroad, 16; Austrian Silesia — Vienna, 21; Trieste, 22; The Adriatic, Coasting Vessels in distress, 23; Pola, 24; Roman Amphitheatre and Temples, 24 ; Corsola and Melida, 25 ; Conversation on the state of the Greek Church, 27 ; Corfu, 28 ; Church of S. Spiridion, 29 ; Ithaca, 30 ; Candia, 30. CHAPTER II. Arrival in Egypt. Alexandria, 31 ; Eastern Sights and Sounds, 31 ; Turkish Bath, 32 ; "Pompey's Pillar", 33 ; Mohammedanism, 34 ; Franciscan Convent, 36 ; Political Parties in Egypt, 37 ; Catacombs in the Desert, 38 ; Roman Pottery, 39 ; Egyptian Music, 40 ; Mahmudie Canal, 41 ; The Nile, 42 ; Grand Cairo, 43 ; Nile Boat, 44; Streets of Cairo, 44; Mosque, 45; Joseph's House, 49; Mehemet Ali's Palace, 50; Old Cairo, 51; The Pyramids, 54 ; Tombs of the Caliphs, 60 ; Ibrahim Pacha's Tomb, 62 ; The Petrified Wood, 63. CHAPTER III. The Nile. metadata.description: Profiles in History: Autograph Auction 34 Winter 2002 Auction Highlights include: Erwin Rommel's raw, triumphant postcard sent on the literal opening week of WWII. Harry Truman's unedited reflections on brawling with Stalin and Churchill at Potsdam. Daniel Boone's hand-drawn Kentucky boundary logs. FDR's localized 1927 ballot where he hand-wrote Eleanor Roosevelt into local office. Presidential & Foundational Era John Adams (December 10, 1799): An exceptionally rare official letter signed as President to the U.S. Senate. Adams explicitly praises the promptitude and zeal of federal troops used to crush the Fries Rebellion in eastern Pennsylvania. The catalog highlights a fascinating backstory: local farmers revolted over direct property taxes passed to fund defense against France. While Adams declared the riot a "highhanded" dangerous affair, he determined it wasn't treason and eventually issued a full pardon—a move that cost him critical support from his own conservative Federalist Party during the tight election of 1800. John Quincy Adams (June 6, 1791): A rare early autograph letter signed to a legal colleague named "Putnam". Written right after his admission to the bar, Adams coordinates a legal writ before playfully adding that the intricate question posed to him is too perplexing for a busy day, proposing they instead discuss it soon over "a segar [cigar] & glass of wine". John Quincy Adams Stock Certificate (April 17, 1809): An original stock certificate for the Boylston Market Association, signed by Adams as its very first president. The historic market complex was built far out of town at the time and named after Adams' second cousin, Ward Nicholas Boylston. James Bowdoin (March 30, 1786): An important Revolutionary War-era letter signed as Governor of Massachusetts to the Governor of North Carolina. Bowdoin officially states that Massachusetts has acceded to Virginia's proposal to hold the Annapolis Convention in Maryland to regulate interstate trade. This meeting ultimately served as the critical precursor to the 1787 Philadelphia Convention, where the weak Articles of Confederation were discarded in favor of the U.S. Constitution. James Buchanan (March 13, 1859): An exceptional pre-Civil War letter signed as President to Indian Affairs Commissioner James Denver. Buchanan voices deep gratitude for Denver's firm, impartial leadership as the territorial Governor of Kansas during the incredibly violent "Bleeding Kansas" border wars. Millard Fillmore (September 15, 1869): A handwritten letter showing a warm kinship between two U.S. presidents. Fillmore writes to voice his deep relief that the newly inaugurated Chief Executive, Ulysses S. Grant, had returned home safely and was on the path to recovering his health after an unexpected illness forced him to miss the New York State Fair. James A. Garfield (April 15, 1881): An exceptionally rare official letter of state signed as President. Garfield authorizes the Secretary of State to affix the Seal of the United States to his formal reply to a congratulatory message from the Republic of San Marino. Because Garfield was tragically shot by an assassin just two and a half months later, documents signed during his brief 6-month presidency are of immense rarity. James A. Garfield on Lincoln's Funeral (May 2, 1865): A poignant handwritten letter written as a Representative from Ohio to Speaker of the House Schuyler Colfax. Garfield writes from his home state to describe traveling to Cleveland to meet Abraham Lincoln’s slow-moving funeral train. He expresses deep regret that Colfax was unable to accompany the cortege, creating an incredible historical link between the first and second U.S. presidents to be assassinated. Andrew Jackson Walking Cane Letter (c. January/February 1831): An exceptional letter signed as President to a Virginia resident, typed out by his adopted son. Jackson warmly accepts a presentation walking cane carved from a tree that stood on the physical battlefield of the Battle of New Orleans. Jackson praises the brave men whose valor served as the "Security of the Union," referencing the legendary War of 1812 victory that vaulted his military persona into the White House. Andrew Jackson Land Grant (January 1, 1830): A document signed as President on vellum, granting a 113-acre plot of land located near St. Louis, Missouri. Thomas Jefferson & the UVA Rotunda (October 7, 1823): A magnificent autograph letter signed from Monticello to Master Carpenter James Oldham. Writing as the "Father of the University of Virginia," the aging former president outlines the ongoing construction of the university's famous architectural crown jewel, the UVA Rotunda. Jefferson rejects Oldham’s direct financial appeals to the Board of Visitors regarding a wage dispute, telling him that contractual adjustments must go through the executive proctor or the ordinary courts. This exact letter famously triggered the very first lawsuit brought against the University of Virginia. Thomas Jefferson Navy Commission (March 16, 1807): An exceptional document signed as President (countersigned by Navy Secretary Robert Smith) commissioning Hethcote J. Reed as a Lieutenant. Reed served as a midshipman on the historic frigate USS Constitution ("Old Ironsides") during the Barbary Coast patrols and fought in the celebrated assault on Tripoli during the Tripolitan War. Thomas Jefferson & James Madison Ships' Papers (December 30, 1806): A large folio-sized safe-passage document signed jointly by Jefferson as President and Madison as Secretary of State. The document features a rare four-language parallel text configuration (English, Dutch, French, and Spanish) granting passage to a brig carrying livestock and lumber out of an American port. William Henry Harrison Political Overtures (July 12, 1837): A dense, 4-page political strategy letter written to Whig organizer Silas M. Stilwell. Harrison plots with party allies Daniel Webster and Henry Clay to overthrow the Jacksonian Democrats in the upcoming 1840 election. Harrison warns his party to respect their opponents' perfect discipline, delivering a timeless political axiom: "Confidence in the weakness of our enemy has produced the most disastrous defeats on record." John F. Kennedy Handwritten Note (January 10, 1962): An incredibly rare autograph letter signed as President on official green White House stationery. Writing to a former Senate colleague ("Senator Martin"), Kennedy sends friendly New Year's greetings, marking one of only a handful of full one-page handwritten presidential letters from JFK in private hands. Herbert Hoover Signed Portrait (Undated): A handsome sepia portrait photograph of the smartly dressed president, warmly inscribed to a local doctor. Herbert Hoover anti-FDR Rant (September 3, 1934): A scathing 2-page typed letter attacking the newly formed "American Liberty League". Hoover accuses the disgruntled corporate Democrats backing the league of hijacking the 1932 Republican platform, bluntly declaring that he has no more confidence in their Wall Street model of liberty than the New Deal model. Herbert Hoover Teapot Dome Speech (November 14, 1933): A signed 5-page transcript of the speech Hoover delivered at the dedication of the Warren G. Harding Memorial. Hoover fiercely castigates the corrupt Teapot Dome conspirators for violating public trust. Historically, Teapot Dome ringleader Harry M. Daugherty sat seething barely thirty feet away in the audience as Hoover spoke. James Madison War-Date Letter (January 5, 1813): A superb presidential letter written marked "private" to his newly elected Vice President, Elbridge Gerry. Madison answers technical questions regarding taking the constitutional oath of office. He urges the aging Gerry to travel south to Virginia to avoid the harsh winter weather, writing: "Your friends in Virginia will then be the gainers..." The catalog highlights that Gerry followed Madison's advice and took his oath at home in Cambridge before taking his seat as president pro tempore of the Senate. This letter is also famous for detailing the origin of the term "gerrymander," coined after Gerry distorted Massachusetts voting districts to look like a salamander. James Madison Cabinet Strife Letter (August 29, 1810): A fascinating autograph letter signed as President to his bitter political rival, Senator Samuel Smith. Madison handles tense complaints regarding Treasury deposits and defends his embattled Treasury Secretary, Albert Gallatin. This letter captures a highly unstable moment in Madison's administration, balancing a divided cabinet alongside a deteriorating relationship with Napoleon on the brink of the War of 1812. James Madison Ship's Passport (June 1, 1811): A scallop-top ship's passport signed on vellum by President Madison, countersigned by Secretary of State Robert Smith, granting safe passage to a two-gun schooner named the Fly of Bristol. James K. Polk Grandfather Vindication (August 24, 1844): A handwritten campaign letter marked "Private" to a Nashville editor. Polk fiercely defends against toxic Whig character attacks that accused his grandfather, Col. Ezekiel Polk, of being a Revolutionary War Tory (a British loyalist). Polk biography notes that Polk became entirely obsessed with this issue, spending more energy defending his grandfather's memory than almost any other topic in the tight 1844 election. Franklin D. Roosevelt Scripture Beliefs (January 6, 1929): A typed letter written as Governor of New York to a Texas reverend, explicitly confirming his deep reliance on the Bible: "Please understand that I read the Scriptures and believe in the Book from cover to cover, and am trying to carry out the teaching of the Master as best I can." Franklin D. Roosevelt Disabled Veterans Message (December 24, 1935): A moving typed letter signed as President, delivered on Christmas Eve to a World War I veterans organization. Roosevelt praises the noble living and noble dead, offering the everlasting gratitude of the nation they served. Franklin D. Roosevelt Dutchess County Absentee Ballot (November 8, 1927): An extraordinary legal voting archive completed and signed three times by FDR just before his election as Governor of New York. Voting an all-Democrat ticket, Roosevelt casts a vote against the extension of the New York Governor's term (a historic irony given he would later break all boundaries by winning four terms as President). Best of all, on the local town section, Roosevelt explicitly hand-writes in his wife, Eleanor Roosevelt, as School Director for Hyde Park. Eleanor Roosevelt on Joseph P. Kennedy (June 21): A rare handwritten letter signed as First Lady to her son James. Eleanor recounts hosting a porch picnic lunch for the Kennedy family patriarch, Joseph P. Kennedy, leaving a sharp and incredibly shrewd historical assessment of the future ambassador: "Joe Kennedy has been here... I enjoyed listening to him. A complete egotist but an intelligent & kindly one." Harry S. Truman on Potsdam & McCarthy (May 28, 1954): A spectacular 6-page autograph letter signed "Harry" to his former Secretary of State, Dean Acheson. Truman recounts working on his memoirs 17 hours a day and relives an exasperated clash he had at the Potsdam Conference with Winston Churchill and Joseph Stalin regarding Spanish dictator Francisco Franco. He tells Acheson that he snapped at the dictators, declaring he didn't come to Berlin to run a "police court". When translated, Stalin roared with laughter and suggested they talk about Poland instead. Truman then transitions to domestic affairs, bluntly observing that the ongoing Sen. Joseph McCarthy anti-communist hearings are causing massive shame to his Republican friends. He sharply criticizes the Eisenhower White House as "smart but inexperienced boys" who are upsetting NATO and throwing away America's military strength while dangerously eyeing intervention in Indo-China. Harry S. Truman on JFK & the 1960 Convention (July 9, 1960): Another remarkable handwritten letter signed "Harry" to Dean Acheson, penned just two days before the 1960 Democratic National Convention. Truman writes that party leaders are begging him to attend, adding that he intends to "have a lot of fun with the guessers and the prophets." The catalog notes that Truman strongly disliked John F. Kennedy, previously calling him too inexperienced and publicly demanding: "Senator, are you certain that you are quite ready for the country?" Woodrow Wilson on the British Blockade (March 19, 1915): A typed letter signed as President, accompanied by a hand-corrected 4-page Letter of State addressed to Great Britain regarding their aggressive naval blockade off Germany. Wilson warns the British government that their unusually massive shipping cordon violates international law by burdening neutral American merchantmen. This warning was terrifyingly on-point: just two weeks later, the German navy retaliated against the blockade zone, sinking the passenger liner Lusitania and drowning nearly 200 Americans. Woodrow Wilson Literature Quote (October 16, 1899): A beautiful, signed autograph quote penned while serving as the President of Princeton University: "Literature is a thing of convictions, of insights, of what is felt and seen and heard and hoped for."Zachary Taylor (June 19, 1850): An incredibly rare letter signed as President, written to New York Governor Hamilton Fish less than one month before Taylor's sudden death in office. Taylor declines an invitation to the New York State Fair, noting that he cannot leave Washington while Congress is aggressively debating the highly controversial Compromise of 1850 regarding the extension of slavery. Taylor fell ill five days after July 4th and passed away from rampaging cholera. William H. Taft on the League of Nations (December 18, 1920): A typed letter signed regarding a controversy over the omission of any reference to God in the preamble to the League of Nations' charter. Taft notes he would have strongly favored a recognition of the Deity, but argues that the omission wasn't sinister and doesn't justify a big debate, concluding: "Preambles are not the substance of the League, and it is about the substance that we are interested." Civil War, Military, & Global Affairs Jefferson Davis (March 20, 1863): A high-stakes Civil War-date letter signed as President of the C.S.A. to Georgia Governor J.E. Brown. Davis addresses a tense military incident where Confederate General Braxton Bragg ordered his quartermasters to use armed force, if necessary, to seize control of Georgia's state-owned Western & Atlantic Railroad after transit workers allegedly refused to transport Southern munitions. Davis acts as an urgent diplomat, regretting the general's extra-legal threats and smoothing over state-versus-federal tensions with a plea for Southern solidarity. Turner Ashby (February 29, 1862): A highly scarce Confederate army receipt signed by Ashby as Colonel in Winchester, Virginia, securing transport wagons and horses. Ashby was one of "Stonewall" Jackson's most trusted cavalry subordinates and was tragically killed in action just three months later. Ellis Spear of the 20th Maine (Undated): A fascinating 5-page original autograph manuscript recounting the close-quarters horrors of the 1864 Wilderness Campaign and the Battle of Spotsylvania Court House. Spear, who took command of the legendary regiment after Joshua Chamberlain was promoted, reflects on the exhausting night marches and constant skirmishes that were enough to make a veteran tired just thinking about it decades later. Joshua L. Chamberlain & Thomas D. Chamberlain (October 12, 1870): A unique historical check filled out by the "Savior of Gettysburg" and signed jointly by both famous brothers. Thomas served as a captain under Joshua, and famously survived a near-fatal close-range gun encounter while successfully securing the Union's left flank on Little Round Top. William F. Smith (March 11, 1891): A candid post-war letter where the former Union Major General admits he is writing a defense paper to evaluate the battlefield performance of General Grant. Smith controversially concludes that General Grant was a poor military commander compared to Confederate generals, echoing a highly unpopular public opinion at the time. Edward Townsend (March 30, 1865): An official State Department invitation presented to the Governor of Missouri to witness the historic flag-raising ceremony at Fort Sumter. Scheduled for April 14, 1865—exactly four years to the day after the fort fell—the event allowed General Robert Anderson to re-raise the very same tattered garrison flag that had marked the literal start of the Civil War. David Ben-Gurion (March 13, 1954): A powerful letter handwritten in Hebrew from his retreat in Sde Boker to a Knesset member. Ben-Gurion issues a stark warning to "naive" pacifists, declaring that Israel must rid itself of illusions that external Jewish organizations can guarantee safety from border raids, fiercely arguing that the sole security of Israel lies with the IDF. Catherine the Great (January 9, 1793): A beautiful, tender New Year's greeting letter written in French by the Russian Empress to her sister, the Princess of Anhalt-Zerbst. Abraham Lincoln Legal Opinion (August 17, 1850): A full-page autograph letter signed from Springfield, Illinois, regarding a civil land title dispute. Evaluating a forged property deed, Lincoln delivers a characteristically blunt and succinct legal assessment: "This is the whole story — The case can not be gained by much talking." Abraham Lincoln Circuit Court Receipt (May 1, 1858): A handwritten financial document signed as an Illinois general practice attorney. Dated just six weeks before his famous "House Divided" speech propelled him to national visibility, Lincoln signs off on court fees received for a case in the Vermilion Circuit Court. Robert E. Lee Lexington Correspondence (June 22, 1866): A gracious 2-page letter written as President of Washington College to a former Union soldier, Major Richard P. Hammond. Writing just one year after the war ended, Lee attempts to track down a missing Confederate general on behalf of his former battlefield adversary, showcasing the smooth, respectful resumption of peace between North and South. Robert E. Lee Signature (March 8, 1869): A bold, clean ink signature reading "R.E. Lee," clipped from a larger document. John Hancock Military Appointment (July 1, 1775): A spectacular Revolutionary War document signed boldly by Hancock as President of the Continental Congress, countersigned by Charles Thomson. Hancock appoints an ensign to the Massachusetts Regiment just two weeks after the bloody Battle of Bunker Hill, and a mere two days before George Washington arrived in Cambridge to assume formal command of the Continental Army. Julia Ward Howe Battle Hymn of the Republic Manuscript (March 21, 1865): A monumental piece of American cultural history. A complete 2-page autograph manuscript of her famous Union rallying anthem, written entirely in her hand and signed just two weeks before Robert E. Lee's surrender at Appomattox. Incredibly, this specific copy features an un-published extra stanza attacking god's contemners that did not make it into the final Atlantic Monthly printing. Francis Gary Powers U-2 Spy Flight Letter (September 22, 1970): A rare typed letter signed by the famous Cold War pilot to an aviation magazine editor. Powers reviews a book tracking the history of aerial reconnaissance, commenting on the super-secret CIA U-2 program that caused an international crisis when he was shot down over downtown Moscow in 1960. Theodor Herzl Zionist Letter (August 10, 1902): A printed political letter signed by the zionist leader from Vienna. Written right as critical negotiations with the Ottoman Empire collapsed, Herzl outlines the upcoming agenda for the Zionist Action Committee, which marked his historic shift to lobby the British government for a Jewish homeland. Nathaniel Lyon Pre-Battle Report (May 12, 1861): An exceptionally rare Civil War letter written from the St. Louis Arsenal just three months before Lyon was killed in action. Writing to the Adjutant General, Lyon reports on a local clash where Union troops and a civilian mob engaged in a deadly shootout, killing 12 people. Lyon openly criticizes his brash superior, General William S. Harney, warning that Harney's erratic city orders painfully embarrass his covert strategy to stop pro-Confederate combinations from seizing the state of Missouri. Philip H. Sheridan Legendary War Horse Letter (March 24, 1876): A wonderful letter penned by the Union hero to an old army comrade. Sheridan reveals that the famous black horse he rode during his frantic, morale-boosting race from Winchester to rally his routed troops at the Battle of Cedar Creek is still alive and well in his possession, noting: "He looks almost as well now as when you saw him in Virginia." Sheridan later renamed the black horse "Winchester." George H. Thomas on the Fitz John Porter Court-Martial (January 5, 1870): An autograph letter signed by the Union general known as "The Rock of Chickamauga." Thomas comments on the infamous Civil War court-martial of Gen. Fitz John Porter, who was relieved of command for alleged dereliction of duty during the Battle of Groveton. Thomas defends Porter's character, stating he never believed Porter willfully neglected his duty. George Washington Free Frank (Undated): A prominent, large ink signature reading "Go: Washington," scrawled as a free-franked address panel to a Connecticut cobbler named Joseph Webb. Historical records indicate Washington wrote to Webb primarily to check on custom orders for "horse skin" boots. George Washington on Long Island Plundering (October 31, 1778): A superb Revolutionary War-date letter signed by the Commander-in-Chief from his headquarters in Fredericksburg. Washington issues a stern reprimand to a local major after learning that Continental scouts traveling to Long Island under the pretext of gathering intelligence were indiscriminately plundering and distressing the local inhabitants. Washington commands him to stop the pernicious practice, explicitly ordering him to only employ those as spies or observers in whom he can place proper confidence. Daniel Boone Fayette County Survey (May 15, 1785): A mind-bogglingly rare complete manuscript document written and signed by the legendary pioneer as a Deputy Surveyor in Fayette County, Kentucky. Boone hand-writes the boundary logs for a 1,000-acre land plot using uncorrected frontier misspellings, tracing lines from "2 Shuger trees" to a "white oke and hickory." Boone tragically lost almost all of his own land in this exact county three years later due to title disputes. Simon Kenton Frontier Warrant (Undated): A financial document signed by the famous trans-Allegheny frontiersman who famously saved Daniel Boone's life during an Indian raid at Boonesborough. Science, Discovery, & Literature Benjamin Franklin (April 9, 1773): A magnificent 2-page autograph letter signed and initialed from London to "Dear Jenky" (Jane Parker). Franklin musters his immense powers of diplomacy to resolve a delicate financial disagreement with the family of his deceased New York printing business partner. To preserve their long family tie, Franklin delivers a timeless piece of advice: "But I think it contributes to the Duration of Friendship to keep its Accounts, & those of Business distinct & separate; and that an exact Justice in Pounds Shillings & Pence should be observed between Friends as between Strangers." Albert Einstein "World State" Manuscript (Undated, Post-WWI): A monumental 3-page unsigned autograph manuscript written in green ink. Einstein maps out a bold political plan for a unified "World State", arguing that the League of Nations failed because member states refused to surrender their individual sovereignty. He argues that a global political system is unconditionally necessary to stop our planet from becoming unbearable for humans, while warning that intellectuals often fail in politics because they lack quick decision-making and human people skills. Tantalizingly, the top of the page features a series of Einstein's handwritten mathematical equations in electromagnetics. Albert Einstein Signed Portrait (1935): A classic black-and-white portrait of Einstein in a tuxedo, beautifully inscribed in German to friends in remembrance of "happy musical evenings" spent playing his beloved violin. John Flamsteed (June 29, 1695): A rare signed financial receipt from the historic first Astronomer Royal of England. Flamsteed's meticulous star mapping directly provided the data Sir Isaac Newton used to verify his legendary theory of gravity. Raymond Chandler (November 5, 1946): A typed letter to his famous Hollywood agent, H.N. Swanson. Written right as Chandler abandoned the stress of the movie studios for the quiet coast of La Jolla, he tracks short story publishing rights while jokingly describing himself as "a guy who never says one thing when four will do." Samuel Francis Smith (December 4, 1893): A wonderful letter from the composer of "My Country, 'Tis of Thee", hoping his anthem kindles a spirit of freedom worldwide. Smith shares a lively reflection on aging, quoting Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.'s birthday tribute to fellow hymn-writer Julia Ward Howe, noting that the human spirit can burn in perpetual youth if kept active. Herman Melville Defending Mardi (June 5, 1849): A magnificent 3-page autograph letter signed to his British publisher Richard Bentley (who would publish Moby-Dick two years later). Melville defends his new novel Mardi, which British critics had violently panned as too abstract and metaphysical, writing a timeless defense of the artist's mind: "But some of us scribblers, my Dear Sir, always have a certain something unmanageable in us, that bids us do this or that, and be done it must – hit or miss." He then reveals he is shifting ground away from the South Seas to write a plain, straightforward, amusing sea narrative with no metaphysics—his semi-autobiographical masterpiece, Redburn: His First Voyage. Melville letters are of legendary rarity. Claude Monet London Illness (March 14, 1901): A poignant 5-page letter handwritten in French on Savoy Hotel stationery to his wife. Monet gripes about a sudden illness that struck him down in London just as he was attempting one last creative effort to capture the Gothic spires of Westminster rising through the changing Thames fog, producing his legendary London Series of impressionist masterpieces. Franklin D. Roosevelt Founding the March of Dimes (April 7, 1927): A historic handwritten letter signed on legal stationery regarding the incorporation of the Georgia Warm Springs Foundation (later known nationwide as the March of Dimes). Paralyzed by polio, FDR details establishing the foundation as a non-profit rehabilitation center to help fellow polio victims find strength, creating one of his most enduring humanitarian health legacies. Jack London on The Call of the Wild (August 28, 1903): A mind-bogglingly rare autograph letter written in pencil to an early reader immediately following the publication of his masterpiece. London explains his creative structure for the novel, revealing his logic behind naming his legendary canine protagonist: "The only reason I named him Buck was that years before I had filed away among my notes as appropriate dog names ‘Buck’ & ‘Bright.’ ... I chose Buck – I guess because it was stronger than Bright." He beautifully adds: "We know little or nothing about what dogs think. But then we may conclude from their actions what their mental processes might be..." West Africa Slave Trade Uprising (January 15, 1808): A terrifying historical letter written by two slave traders aboard the Ship Hibernia near the St. Paul's River in Sierra Leone. Writing at the absolute peak of the Atlantic slave trade, they describe a massive, violent slave uprising where hundreds of local fighters descended upon their factory staging fort, plundering the stores, cutting the trader's hand, and forcing them to flee under cover of night. Letters detailing slave trade mutinies written directly from Africa are of immense historical scarcity. Hollywood, Sports, & Pop Culture Dwight D. Eisenhower (November 22, 1944): A deeply moving wartime letter written from Versailles to his wife, Mamie. The Supreme Allied Commander handles regular family business—enclosing $25 to help buy a durable Christmas gift for their son—before offering a somber look at the front lines: "Well sweet I’d like to think that this mess would be over soon... But the fighting and the dying go on – and the end is not yet. ‘Civilization’ is not pretty, when it resorts to war." Josephine Earp (March 3, 1929): An incredibly rare autograph letter signed by the wife of legendary gunfighter Wyatt Earp. Written just months after Wyatt's death, the former actress coordinates travel details while defending her late husband's untamed frontier legacy. Thomas Edison on Theodore Roosevelt (April 1919): An original autograph note scrawled on a poem written by a 13-year-old girl honoring the late President. Edison writes in pencil: "Some Girl! It’s in the blood capacity for high mental action accompanies the germ plasm..." 1951 Brooklyn Dodgers Signed Baseball: An official ball signed by 22 legendary members of the team, including Chuck Dressen, Gil Hodges, Pee Wee Reese, and Jackie Robinson. This historic ball dates to the exact, infamous season that culminated in Ralph Branca giving up the pennant-winning "Shot Heard 'Round the World" home run to the rival Giants. Ty Cobb Batting Advice Letter (September 14, 1954): A massive 5-page strategy letter written in green ink by "The Georgia Peach" to Pirates manager Fred Haney. Cobb offers dense, un-asked-for advice to pull a struggling hitter out of a slump, detailing exact hand placements, swinging parallels, and a warning to stop swinging for the fences. Cooperstown Hall of Fame Signed Bat: An official souvenir baseball bat signed boldly on the barrel by 13 legendary titans, including Ted Williams, Mickey Mantle, Willie Mays, Hank Aaron, and a highly controversial addition by Pete Rose. Irving Berlin Signed Sheet Music (1938): Vintage sheet music for "Alexander's Ragtime Band", beautifully inscribed by Berlin to fellow Academy Award-nominated Hollywood film composer Lew Pollack. Lucille Ball (Undated): A gorgeous sepia publicity photograph featuring her resting elegantly on a ship's helm, signed with warm sentiments. Josephine Baker (1935): A spectacular, oversized vintage photograph of the exotic stage dancer captured mid-performance, signed with a bold French inscription. P.T. Barnum (November 30, 1887): A beautiful letter written to a young boy, where the legendary showman lovingly promises that his traveling circus, "The Greatest Show on Earth", will be even larger, funnier, and more marvelous next year. George Gershwin An American in Paris Photograph (March 1929): An extraordinary sepia portrait showing the legendary composer seated at his piano. In the lower margin, Gershwin beautifully pens an autograph musical quotation consisting of four bars of music, mapping out the famous primary orchestral theme of An American in Paris just three months after its Carnegie Hall debut. Ira Gershwin MGM Movie Contract (December 27, 1949): A historic 6-page studio contract signed by the legendary lyricist for the Academy Award-winning MGM musical An American in Paris. The contract maps out his $56,250 pay structure and includes the famous studio "morals and conduct" clause used to keep contract players under the studio's thumb. John F. Kennedy & Robert Frost Inaugural Booklet (April 1961): A unique presentation copy of the limited-edition booklet printed for Robert Frost’s White House reception. It features Frost's dedication poem alongside the full text of JFK's historic "Ask not what your country can do for you" speech. It is signed by Kennedy on the cover and features a warm inscription from Frost to a journalist friend detailing the plane flight they shared. Ernest Hemingway Overseas Background Check (Undated): A jovial letter handwritten entirely in pencil to his hunting buddy Charles Thompson—the direct inspiration for "Karl" in The Green Hills of Africa. Hemingway requests that Thompson serve as a character witness for a government background check so he can travel overseas, writing with his signature wit: "If they interrogate you you can tell them what a good patriot, swell guy, always pay my debts (within two years or 20)..."Jerome Kern Signed Sheet Music (May 19, 1938): Vintage sheet music for the song "You Couldn't Be Cuter", inscribed to fellow film composer Lew Pollack. It is accompanied by a funny typed letter where Kern jokes that the song will probably be a "mummy by Decoration Day". Alex Haley Roots Inscription (June 25, 1984): A signed card featuring a good-natured sentiment referencing his ground-breaking saga, sending brotherly love from "Chicken George" and the family of Kunta Kinte. California Gold Rush Prospector Letter (July 25, 1849): A fascinating 3-page letter written by early 49er Mason R. Packer from Stockton, California, to his wife back east. Packer notes the exorbitant prices of basic goods in the boomtowns and coordinates his departure for the gold diggings near Sutter's Fort. The Honeymooners Cast Signed Photograph: A vintage publicity still showing the four core cast members (Jackie Gleason, Audrey Meadows, Art Carney, and Joyce Randolph) hanging out of a New York City bus window, signed beautifully by each actor. Charles Lindbergh Aviation Matte Portrait (Undated): A striking, oversized sepia waist-up portrait captured by Underwood & Underwood, showing Lindbergh standing proudly with the Spirit of St. Louis in the background, signed cleanly on the photographer's matte. Charles Lindbergh Leather Flight Portrait (Undated): A magnificent head-and-shoulders sepia portrait showing the youthful aviator clad in his complete leather flight jacket, helmet, and goggles, signed in bold black ink. Both Lindbergh portraits originated directly from the estate of the nation's very first federal aviation regulator, William P. MacCracken. The Little Rascals Vintage Signatures (1938–1939): A rare and highly desirable collector's set of five individual autograph leaves signed by the core childhood stars of the fabled Hal Roach Our Gang comedies, including Spanky McFarland, Buckwheat, Alfalfa, Darla Hood, and Porky Lee. Willie Mosconi Signed Billiard Ball Set: A complete presentation box containing fifteen individual billiard balls and an accompanying cue ball, each signed in full by the perennial 15-time world champion. The catalog notes his historic 1954 exhibition record where he sank an unbelievable 526 consecutive pool balls without a single miss. George S. Patton Cadet Letters (c. Fall 1903): A beautiful early letter written as a young cadet attending the Virginia Military Institute (VMI) to his aunt. Exhibiting his lifelong obsession with historical military tactics, the future general explicitly asks her to bring him white writing paper (rejecting blue paper as un-military) along with a newly published textbook entitled Strategy as Illustrated in British Campaigns. Richard Nixon Anti-Communist Speech (c. April 1953): A massive 15-page original typed speech layout containing extensive handwritten corrections and segregation notes by Vice President Richard Nixon. Plunging into a aggressive defense of his controversial role hunting down hidden Communists on the House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC), Nixon defends the Alger Hiss investigations and prophetically maps out future international relations in East Asia. Roy Rogers & Gabby Hayes Signed Photo: A vintage 8x10 black-and-white publicity still showing both iconic Western screen stars in full costume, signed boldly across the image. Albert Schweitzer Aspen Visit (July 7, 1949): A striking portrait photograph of the philosopher and medical missionary, signed and dated during his historic summer visit to Aspen, Colorado. Piotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky Signed Cabinet Photo: An exceptional sepia vignette portrait photograph signed boldly across the image in Cyrillic script. The catalog hails this piece as perhaps the finest signed visual artifact of the legendary romantic composer in existence. Harriet Beecher Stowe Signed Quote: A crisp ink signature by the abolitionist author of Uncle Tom's Cabin, penning a biblical quote: "Trust in the Lord and do good." Booker T. Washington Tuskegee Appeal (January 27, 1894): A letter written on official school stationery to a New York judge. The iconic educator appeals for financial tuition sponsorships for poor but worthy Black students, written just one year prior to his historic "Atlanta Compromise" race-relations address. Mark Twain Faded Portrait (April 1909): A beautiful sepia-tone portrait showing the elderly humorist seated in a wooden chair, affectionately signed and inscribed: "Truly yours, Mark Twain. For Elizabeth."Elizabeth Taylor Nibbles and Me Hardcover (1946): A rare copy of the children's book written and illustrated entirely by a 13-year-old Elizabeth Taylor immediately following her breakout success in National Velvet. The book is warmly inscribed on the inside cover: "Lots of Love – From Nibbles & Elizabeth." Global Conflict & World War II Relics Erwin Rommel "Desert Fox" Postcard (September 9, 1939): A historic, mint-condition postcard handwritten in German by Rommel to his wife, Lucia Mollin, just eight days after the Nazi invasion of Poland sparked World War II. Rommel marvels at his new assignment commanding Hitler's guard battalion, writing with chilling confidence: "Things are going amazingly well for me... If we manage to maintain this pace, the war will be over in the West by the end of October, in my opinion." Admiral Chester Nimitz Propaganda handbill (February 1945): A wartime typed letter signed by Fleet Admiral Nimitz to an 1.1-year-old girl who shared his birthday. As a gift, Nimitz encloses an authentic U.S. propaganda bill dropped by Allied bombers over the Japanese mainland. The item is a 10-yen note printed on the back with a Japanese warning blasting the military cartel for wasting 5,000 yen per person on a losing war. Captured Okinawa "Rising Sun" Flag: An original silk Japanese military banner captured during the brutal Battle of Okinawa by a U.S. Army Major. The flag features printed margins translating to fierce nationalist slogans: "Our Military Strength Will Last Forever" and "Hoping for a Quick War." Gregory "Pappy" Boyington Flying Tigers Jacket: The authentic, black satin reversible flight jacket acquired directly from the estate of the legendary Marine Corps flying ace. The breast features embroidered stylized birds, the back showcases a fierce yellow tiger, and the reverse side maps out a detailed quilted green chart labeling major Japanese target cities around Mount Fuji. Charlie Owens D-Day Mapping Board (April 7, 1944): An original large perspective drawing accomplished in ink and pastel by the Los Angeles Times sketch artist. Dated exactly two months prior to the Allied invasion, the journalistic map utilizes sweeping arrows to project the exact troop movement paths that would be used on D-Day. Chaim Weizmann Palestine University Letter (July 10, 1903): A typed letter signed by the future first President of Israel, mapping out early zionist circulars to advocate for the foundation of a Jewish university in Palestine to combat academic discrimination in Europe.

metadata.description: Approved For Release 2007/01/16: CIA-R57-00384R001200010012-6 -STATEMENT OF THE MANAGERS ON THE PART OF THE HOUSE The managers on the part of the House at the conference on the disagreeing votes of the two Houses on the amendments of the Senate to the.bill (H. R. 4473) to provide revenue, and for other purposes, submit the following statement in explanation of the effect of the action agreed upon by the conferees and recommended in the accompanying conferen:co report: Amendment No. 1: The House bill provided for an increase in individual income-tax rates by a percentage increase of 12j2 percent of the tax liability under existing law, with an over-all effective ceiling rate of 90 percent of the net income of the taxpayer. The House bill also increased the alternative tax on capital gains by 12'22 percent. The Senate amendment eliminated the increase in the alternative tax on capital gains and provided, in general, for an increase of 11 percent of the present tax liability, or 8 percent of the amount by which the surtax net income exceeds present taxes, whichever produced the lesser increase in tax. The Senate amendment provided an over-all ceiling rate of 88 percent of the net income of the taxpayer. Under the conference agreement the increase in the combined nor- mal tax and surtax under existing law will, in general, be 11% percent of the present rates or 9 percent of the amount by which the surtax net income exceeds present taxes, whichever is the lesser. Special rates are provided for the calendar year 1951 so as to reflect Novem- ber 1, 1951, as the effective date of the increase in tax. The coiling rate of 88 percent contained in the Senate amendment is retained under the conference agreement, and no increase in tax is provided with respect to the alternative tax on capital gains. Under the House bill no termination date was provided for the increase in the taxes. The Senate amendment provided for the termination of the increased rates on January 1, 1954, and the conference agreement retains the termination date. Amendments Nos. 2 and 3: These amendments are clerical. The Senate recedes. Amendments Nos. 4 and 5: The House bill provided for an increase in the normal tax on corporations, in general, from 25 to 30 percent of normal tax net income, applicable to taxable years beginning after December 31, 1950. The Senate provided for an increase in the cor- poration normal tax from 25 to 27 percent and an increase in the corporation surtax from 22 to 25 percent. Under the Senate amend- ment, the increases in normal tax and surtax were to be effective as of April 1, 1951, and were to terminate on December 31, 1953. Spe- cial rates were provided for the calendar year 1951 to reflect the April 1 effective date. Under the conference agreement on amend- ments 4 and 5, the normal tax is increased from 25 to 30 percent as provided in the House bill with no increase in the surtax. The in- crease in normal tax is to be effective as of April 1, 1951, with a normal tax rate of 28% percent for the calendar year 1951. The conference Approved For Release 2007/01/16: CIA-R?P57-00384R001200010012-6 Approved For Release 2007/01/16: CIA-RDP57-00384R001200010012-6 REVENUE ACT OF 1951 agreement provides that the, increase in normal tax is to terminate as of March 31, 1954. . Amendment No. 6: The House bill amended section 430 (a) (2) of the code (relating to maximum excess profits tax) so as to increase the percentage used under existing law for computing the maximum excess profits tax from 62 to 70 percent. The Senate amendment provided a new method for computing the maximum excess profits tax which, in general, was 16% percent of the excess profits net income for the calendar year 1951 and was 17 percent of the excess profits net income for taxable years beginning after March 15, 1951. The 17 percent figure of the Senate amendment was comparable to a 69 percent figure under the method provided in the House bill. Tie House recedes with an amendment which adopts the Senate method of computing the maximum tax but increases. the 17 percent figure to 18 percent (comparable to the House bill .70 percent figure) for taxable years beginning after March 31., 1951. Under the conference agreement the maximum excess profits tax for the calendar year 1951 is 1T/4 percent of the excess profits net income for such year. Amendments Nos. 7, 8, and 9: Senate amendments Nos. 7 and g amended section 207 (a) (tax on certain insurance companies), 362 (b) (tax on regulated investment companies), section 421 (a) (tax on business income of certain tax exempt organizations), and section. 26 (relating to credits for corporations) of the code to make changes conforming to the action of the Senate with respect to the corporate normal and surtax rate increases. These amendments also made other technical conforming changes in the code. Senate amend- ment No. 9 struck out section 123 of the House bill which provided for the allowance of only one surtax exemption and one minimum excess profits credit to certain controlled groups of corporations. The House recedes on amendments Nos. 7 and 8 with conforming amend- ments and an amendment adding a new section 1.5 (c) to the code (relating to disallowance of surtax exemptions and minimum excess profits credit) and the House roc: des on amendment No. 9. The new subsection (c) of section 15 applies to the situation where a corporation, on or after January 1., 1951, transfers property (other than money) to one or more corporations created 'for the purpose of acquiring such property, or to one or more corporations not actively engaged in business at the time of such acquisition, if after such transfer the. transferor corporation or its stockholders, or both, are in control of the transferee during any part of a taxable ye sr of such transferee corporation. In such case the transferee corporation shall not be allowed either the $25,000 exemption from surtax or the $25,000 minimum excess profits credit unless it establishes by the clear pro[Ondprancc. of the evidence that the securing of the $25,000 exe m.ption or the $25,000 minimum excess profits credit, or both, was not a major purpose of the transfer of the property to it by the transferor. The term "control" is defined as the ownership of stock possessing at least 80 percent of the total combined voting power of all classes of stock entitled to vote or at least 80 percent of the total value of shares of all classes of stock of the corporation. Under the amendment the ownership of stock is to be determined in accordance with the provisions of section 503, except that constructive owner- ship under section 503 (a) (2) is to be determined only -with' respect to the individual's spouse and minor children. The Secretary, to the Approved For Release 2007/01/16: CIA-RDP57-00384R001200010012-6 Approved For Release 2007/01/16: CIA-RDP57-00384R001200010012-6 extent not inconsistent with the provisions of the new subsection, is granted the same authority as under section 129 (b) to allow in whole or in part a surtax exemption or a minimum excess profits credit which might otherwise be disallowed under the subsection or to apportion such exemption or credit among the corporations in- volved. For example: Corporation A transfers on January 1, 1952, all of its property to corporations B and C in exchange for the entire stock of such corporations. Immediately thereafter corporation A is dissolved, its stockholders becoming the stockholders of B and C. Assuming that a major purpose for such transfers is to secure addi- tional surtax exemptions and minumum excess profits credits, the Secretary has the authority to allow one such exemption and credit and to apportion such exemption and credit between corporations B and C. It is provided that the subsection shall not be applicable to any taxable year with respect to, which the tax imposed by sub- chapter D of chapter 1 (relating to the excess profits tax) is not in effect. It is not intended that the new subsection shall in any way delimit or abrogate any of the existing provisions of the code (including sec. 129), or any principle established by judicial decision, which have the effect of preventing the avoidance of income or excess profits taxes. Amendment No. 92: This amendment, for which there is no cor- responding provision in the bill as it passed the House, amends section 127 of the code to provide an alternative treatment of war loss re- coveries, applicable at the election of the taxpayer. Under the amend- ment the amount of the recovery, to the extent that it does not exceed the allowable deductions in prior taxable years on account of the destruction or seizure of property in respect of which the recovery is received, is excluded from gross income for the taxable year in which the recovery is received. In lieu of including such amount in gross income for the taxable year of the recovery, there is to be added to the tax imposed by chapter 1 for such taxable year the total increase in the tax under chapter 1 and chapter 2 for all taxable years which would result by decreasing, in an amount equal to such part of the recovery so excluded, deductions allowable in prior taxable years with respect to the destruction or seizure of the property. To the extent that the amount of the recovery exceeds the allowable de- ductions in prior taxable years on account of the destruction or seizure of the property, such amount is treated for the taxable year of the re- covery as gain on the involuntary conversion of property and is recog- nized or nonrecognized as provided in section 112 (f). This amend- ment also provides a new rule for the determination of the unadjusted basis of property where the alternative treatment of the recovery is, applicable pursuant to election made by the taxpayer. The House recedes with amendments which revise section 127 (c) (3) (A) and (5), and make minor changes in the phrasing of section 127 (c) (3) (B) and (C) and section 127 (d) (2). The effective date of the amend- ment is also changed so that it will be applicable to taxable years be- ginning after December 31, 1941. Section 127 (c) (3) (A), relating to the definition of "amount of recovery" for the purposes of the new alternative treatment, is revised under the conference agreement so that in the case of recovery of the same property or interest considered under section 127 (a) as destroyed or seized, such property or interest may be included in the amount of recovery at its fair market value, determined as of the date of recovery, or at the option of the taxpayer at the adjusted basis (for determining loss) of such property or interest in the hands of the tax- payer on the date of the loss. Under the Senate amendment, the maximum tax would not exceed. the following percentages of the first $400,000 of the excess profits net income: 5 percent if the taxable year is the first or second taxable year (determined from the commencement of business), 8 percent for the third. taxable year, 11 percent for the fourth taxable year, and 14 percent for the fifth taxable year. Under the Senate amend- ment, if, for any such year the excess profits net income exceeds $400,000, the excess over $400,000 is subject to the same maximum tax as in the case of other corporations. The amendment also provides rules in subsection (e) (2) for deter- mining, for the purpose of the, subsection, when, a taxpayer shall be considered to have commenced business and to have had taxable years determined by reference to the date of commencem?nt of busi- ness of certain other corporations. It contemplates that the Secre- tary will, by regulations, provide for the determination of construc- tive taxable years by reference to the annual accounting period first established by the taxpayer. The Senate amendment also provides, in effect, that the benefits of the special limitation provisions under section 430 (e) (1) shall be denied to any taxpayer which derives more than 50 percent of its income for the taxable year from contracts or subcontracts to which title I of the Renegotiation Act of 1951 or to which any prior renegotia- tion act is applicable. The House recedes with an amendment. Paragraph (1) of subsec- tion (e) is amended to make it clear that the provision is applicable only to taxpayers whose fifth taxable year ends after June 30, 1950. Clauses (ii) and (iii) of subparagraph (E) of subsection (e) (1) are amended to conform the percentage figures specified therein to those provided by the conference agreement on Senate Amendment No. 6. An additional amendment is made to clause (ii) of such subparagraph to make clear that, for the purpose of such clause, a person shall not be considered a member of it group of persons who control the taxpayer and another corporation unless during the period specified in such clause he owns stock in the corporation at a, time when the members of the group control such corporation and he owns stock in the taxpayer at a time when the. members of the group con- trol the taxpayer. A change is made in subparagraph (B) of para- graph (2) of subsection (e) to the effect that transactions described in clauses (i) and (iii) shall be disregarded in determining the date as of which the taxpayer shall be considered to have commenced busi- ness if the adjusted basis of the aggregate assets acquired by the taxpayer in such transactions before December 1, 1950 (or acquired in the ordinary course of business in replacement of such assets), constituted less than. 20 percent of the adjusted basis of the taxpayer's total assets as of December 1, 1950. A change is also made in para- graph (3) of subsection (e) to provide, that the gross income of the taxpayer for the taxable year from contracts and subcontracts sub- ject to renegotiation shall, for the purpose of applying the limitation provided by such paragraph, be determined without regard to capital gains and dividends received.. Such gross income is the gross income after renegotiation. Amendment No. 220: This amendment, for which there is no cor- responding provision in the House bill, provides for exclusion in the computation of excess profits not income, for both excess profits tax taxable years and base, period years, of payments made to a domestic corporation by its related, foreign corporation as remuneration for certain technical services rendered. The House recedes with clarifying amendments and an amendment which amends the definition of related foreign corporation to provide that, in order to be It related corporation, 10 percent or more of the stock of the foreign corporation must be owned by the domestic corporation at the time the specified services are rendered. Amendment iNTo. 221: This amendment adds section 503 to the, bill, for which. there is no corresponding section in the House bill. This section permits a taxpayer with a. fiscal year beginning before January 1, 1950, and ending after March 31, 1950, in computing its average base period net income under the general average method provided by sec- tion 435 (d) of time code, to use the period of 48 consecutive months ending March 31, 1950, instead of its base period, if such computation produces a lesser excess profits tax for the taxable year. Amendment No. 222: This amendment extends to a new corpora- tion which commenced business before the end of its base period the right. to qualify under section 435 (e) of the code for the alternative average base period net income based on growth for the purpose of determining its excess profits credit based on income. The House recedes with technical amendments. Amendment No. 223: This amendment extends the benefits of sec- tion 435 (e) (2) (G) (special alternative average base period net income for a corporation whose excess profits net income: for 1949 is not more than 25 percent of its excess profits net income for 1948) to a taxpayer qualifying for growth treatment under section 435 (e) (1) (B) even though it also qualifies as a growth corporation under section 435 (e) (1) (A). The House recedes. Amendment No. 224: This amendment, for which there is no corresponding section in the House bill, provides limitations in the case of a bank, as defined in section 104 of the code, on the amount of the inadmissible asset adjustment to the net capital addition or re- duction for the taxable year, to the net new capital addition for the tax- able year, and to the base period capital addition. This amendment also amends section 435 (f) (relating to capital additions in the base period) to make clear that the yearly base period capital. of any tax- payer (whether or not a bank) shall not be reduced below zero by the inadmissible asset adjustment. . The House recedes with clarifying amendments and with an amend- ment dealing with the effective date of the provision applicable to the base period capital addition of banks, making such provision retro- active only at the election of the taxpayer. Amendment No. 225: This amendment, for which there is no corre- sponding provision in the House bill, adds two new paragraphs (9) and (10) to section 435 (g) (relating to net capital addition or reduc- tionn) in order to provide, if certain conditions are met, that a decrease in inadmissible assets, to the extent in excess of the net capital reduc- tion (if any) for the taxable year, shall be an addition to the excess profits credit computed under the income method. The principal condition to be met is that where there is a decrease in inadmissible assets there must also be a corresponding increase in operating assets before any increase in the credit is allowed. The House recedes with clarifying amendments and with an amend- ment providing a special rule for the treatment of a decrease in inadmissible assets in the case of a bank. Amendment No. 226: This amendment, for which there is no corresponding provision in the bill as passed by the House, permits a dealer in wholly tax-exempt Government securities to elect to increase its excess profits net income by the interest (with certain adjustments) on such obligations, and to treat sucl3 obligations as admissible assets. The House recedes with a technical amendment and an amendment which extends the application of the section to Government obliga- tions any part of the interest from which is allowable as a credit against net income. The report deals with the situation in the Egyptian Armed Forces and Egyptian Army strategy after the signing of the peace treaty with Israel. The report indicates that the Egyptian Army strategy, especially since President Husni Mubarak assumed power after Al-Sadat's assassination, has been to introduce advanced weapons to the art of military combat, and that Egyptian arms in this regard have not been confined to those imported from the United States, since Egyptian military officials and their political leadership realize that the United States would not allow the Egyptian Army's modernization except within a framework that the U.S. Administration would allow, and which in turn would not affect Israel's secu- rity. The Egyptian Army disapproves utterly of the special and distinct military relationship between the United States and Israel. The report goes on to say: In view of this, Egypt has decided to seek assistance from the European states, both Western and Eastern; it has also initiated military cooperation with the Soviet Union. The report stresses that cooperation will rapidly double within. the coming years. The report therefore warned the U.S. Government about the consequences of allowing Soviet-Egyptian cooperation to reach its maximum with- out any clear U.S. intervention to obstruct this form of military cooperation! The report reviewed the strategies of the Egyptian Army at this stage, indicating that Egypt has turned to the system of integrated military cities, a kind of modern- ization designed to give a secret nature to military training and to maintain the continuity of military lines, as is now happening in the two cities of Junayfah and Shallufah. This is in addition to a building plan being prepared by the Egyptian Defense Ministry covering the areas of Al-'Amiriyah, Dahshur, Inshas, and Al-Hayk- stib. Teacher Arrested, Accused of Spying for Israel NC101228 Cairo MENA in Arabic 1212 GMT 10 Jan 88 [Text] Cairo, 10 Jan (MENA)-MENA has learned that `Abd al-Hamid Subh Labbad, an Egyptian teacher, has been arrested and charged with working as an agent for Israel and with supplying that country with vital infor- mation about Egypt, particularly military information. Security services had informed the Higher State Security Prosecution Office about the defendant's activities. The Higher State Security Prosecution subsequently ordered the man's arrest. Interior Minister on Arrest of `Leftist' Group JN072324 Cairo AL-AHRAM in Arabic 5Jan88pp1, 10 [Excerpt] Interior Minister Zaki Badr has announced that a new leftist organization has been arrested. He said that the organization will be unveiled soon. During a meeting with the head and members of the academic staff at Al-Mansurah University, Badr said that a profes- sor at Asyut University distributed leaflets among the students and showed a film comparing Islam and Chris- tianity before students at the academic staff club. He said this had resulted in a sectarian sedition. He added that the demonstrations organized by some religious leaderships last Friday were aimed at setting ablaze the Jewish synagogue and public places and shops on Cairo streets. The minister added that the aim of religious and leftist groups is against the regime in Egypt. He said that they are trying to control the professional unions in order to achieve their objectives. He affirmed that the mission of university professors is educating the youths. He denied demanding the cancellation of university academic staff clubs, but he demanded that the board of directors of four academic clubs be dissolved for violating the laws. They are the academic staff clubs of the Cairo, Alexan- dria, Al-Mansurah, and Asyut Universities. The minister said that the opposition forces want to win the support of national establishments and unions in order to use them to achieve their objectives of causing incitement and casting doubts. He said that party activ- ity has its own sectors, and that nobody has the right to penetrate the national institutions to distract them from their national mission. The minister expressed appreciation for the university professors. He said he holds the greatest respect for them. He said he blames some of them for encouraging students to stage demonstrations outside universities. This disturbs security and order, although they know that the demonstrating students will be firmly and strongly confronted. The minister urged the professors to teach the students the right way to express their opinions through the legitiamte channels. Concerning the implementation of the emergency law, the minister said that it made it possible to arrest drug dealers who annually purchase $6 billion worth of drugs to destroy citizens' lives. The minister responded to a request by the Al-Mansurah University academic staff to establish a services unit inside the campus, including a unit for car licenses and passports. We must move toward civil disobedience. I address this call to the Palestinian Arab masses in the occupied territories, and to the honest patriotic Palestin- ian leaders, and to the universities, colleges, schools, social centers, press centers, press associations, and to the free journalists and to the camps, trade unions, associations, people's committees, associations, societies and clubs, and to the mosques and churches. To all of them I address my call. I call on all preachers in these mosques and churches; I call on all the masses of those who will pray in occupied Palestine; I call on all students, male and female, and I call on all patriotic leaders to move toward civil disobedience and to avoid violence. It is a pop- ular rejection that I am calling upon you to carry out; popular disobedience to be carried out by the masses. The popular disobedience includes civil disobedience, that is, cutting off water supplies to the enemy's camps in the occupied territories as much as possible, cutting off electricity, roads, secret sabotage, like those who inserted pins in the oranges to be shipped abroad. There are small and very small means that we want every Palestinian to use for secret sabotage. Civil disobedience must be declared and we should take it to the streets without using any violence, this time without even a cigarette, we must sit in the streets, sleep in the streets, make our social meetings in the streets and our parties in the streets. Weddings and funerals should be held in the streets; whoever can sleep should sleep in the street. This is what the Camp David agreement stipulated. The Egyp- tian regime, which is implementing the agreement, can- not get out of it. We should continue to hear each other and to talk to each other until victory. It is a revolution until victory. The people's will should be stronger than the bullets. metadata.description: PAYSAGES DE LA BIBLE : VUES DES LIEUX LES PLUS REMARQUABLES MENTIONNÉS DANS L'ANCIEN ET LE NOUVEAU TESTAMENT. Vers 1832, J. M. W. Turner (1775-1851) a reçu une commande pour vingt-six vues de paysages bibliques à graver par les frères Finden en association avec John Murray. Turner et les autres artistes commandités n'avaient jamais visité la Terre Sainte, ils ont donc basé leurs dessins sur des esquisses prises sur place par des voyageurs tels que les architectes Charles Barry (1795-1860), et Charles Robert Cockerell (1788-1863), Henry Gally Knight (1786–1846) et Sir Robert Ker Porter (1777–1842). Après Turner, les artistes les plus importants employés pour achever les oeuvres étaient Augustus Wall Callcott (1779-1844) et William Clarkson Stanfield (1793-1867). La première édition, publiée par John Murray en 1834, s'intitulait T he Biblical Keepsake ou Landscape Illustrations of the Most Remarkable Places Mentioned in the Holy Scriptures (note de tate.org.uk : catalogue entry [from] Finden's 'Landscape Illustrations of the Bible' pub.1834–6 ). Entre les années 1829 et 1837, l’œuvre de Turner va évoluer de manière encore plus radicale pour s'intéresser de moins en moins à la réalité figurative, et ne garder qu'une vision lumineuse et transfigurée de celle-ci ... impressionniste.net . Gravures de William Finden (1787-1852), Edward Francis Finden (1791–1857), James Baylis Allen (1803–1876) et James Stephenson (1808–1886). Vol 1 ( volume 2 ). Londres J. Murray & Ch. Tilt. 1836. Citations et descriptions par le Révérend Thomas Hartwell Horne. PDF - iBOOK - Gravures > JPEG (2845x2145) ci-contre.
